messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 46
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: Oceania
- Relationship Status: Widowed
- Occupation: Auditor
- Trauma Type: Natural disaster
- Pcl5: 41

**Patient Name:** Mr. Tane A.
**Age:** 46
**Occupation:** Auditor
**Trauma:** 2023 Cyclone Lusi (Category 5 storm surge)

Mr. Tane is a quiet man who sits with his hands folded in his lap, his gaze often drifting to the window of my office. He is an auditor for a regional government agency, a job he describes as “fitting for a man who likes things to add up.” He came to see me six months after the cyclone, at the insistence of his sister, who found him sleeping in his car in the garage.

The story begins on a Tuesday evening, two years ago. Mr. Tane and his wife, Leilani, lived in a coastal village on an island in the South Pacific. Leilani was a marine biologist, and their home was a two-story wooden house fifty meters from the shore. They had weathered storms before. But Cyclone Lusi was different. The warning came late. By the time the winds hit, the sea had already swallowed the beach.

He tells me about the sound. Not the wind, but the water. A deep, grinding roar that he can still feel in his chest. He and Leilani moved to the second floor. The water followed, rising up the stairs. He remembers the smell—salt, diesel from a ruptured boat, and wet wood. He held Leilani’s hand as the house began to tilt. A wave, he says, “came through the wall like a fist.” It tore her from his grip.

He found her body the next morning, tangled in the branches of a banyan tree, a kilometer inland. He carried her back to what was left of their street. He did not cry. He did not scream. He simply found a dry piece of pavement and sat with her until the relief team arrived.

In the months that followed, Mr. Tane rebuilt his life like a spreadsheet. He moved to the capital city, found a new job as an auditor, and rented a small, windowless apartment on the fourth floor of a concrete building. He told himself he was fine. He had a routine. He woke at 5:30 AM, made instant coffee, and reviewed expense reports for eight hours. He ate the same meal every night: white rice and canned tuna.

But the numbers stopped adding up. He tells me that three months ago, he was auditing a travel claim for a colleague who had taken a ferry. The word “ferry” triggered a flashback so vivid he vomited into his trash can. He now avoids any document with the word “water” or “storm.” He has started taking the stairs at work because the elevator reminds him of being trapped in the flooding house. He has lost fourteen pounds because he cannot eat fish—the smell of it makes him gag.

At night, he does not sleep. He lies awake, listening. Every drip from a faucet is the sound of rising water. Every gust of wind against his window is the roar of the cyclone. He has stopped showering because the sensation of water on his skin makes his heart pound so hard he feels he might die. He washes with a damp cloth, standing on a towel to avoid any puddles.

His sister found him in the car because he had started driving to the coast at 2 AM. He does not remember doing it. He will wake up in the driver’s seat, parked on a cliff overlooking the ocean, his hands white-knuckled on the wheel. He tells me he is not suicidal. He just needs to see the water. He needs to prove it is not coming for him. But every time he looks at the horizon, he sees Leilani’s face, and he hears that grinding roar.

He is a man who built his life on precision and order, and he is now drowning in a chaos he cannot audit. He sits in my office, still as a stone, and says, “I used to know how to make things balance. Now I don’t even know what the equation is.”
